title: Does Location Matter? A Black-Box Causal Audit RevealsModel-Dependent Audio Grounding in LALM Hallucination

paper.title: Does Location Matter? A Black-Box Causal Audit Reveals Model-Dependent Audio Grounding in LALM Hallucination
paper.abstract:
Abstract Large audio-language models (LALMs) frequently hallucinate sounds that are not present. Audio-Aware Decoding (AAD) [ 10 ] contrasts logits under the real recording against an
all-zero “blank” waveform, which is out-of-distribution and conflates
“evidence absent” with “input malformed.” We introduce a black-box
causal test: localize the region a claim would rely on with CLAP,
remove only that region via spectral gating, and compare against an
equally-sized random window, on three LALMs. On Qwen2-Audio-7B
( n = 4355 n{=}4355 ), localized ablation’s raw AUROC trails blank’s (0.613 vs. 0.721); we show this is a duration confound: a duration-only
regression predicts blank’s mean effect almost exactly ( 0.067 0.067 vs. 0.071 0.071 ), and holding duration fixed, localized ablation beats random
removal at every grid cell, on both models. On Audio Flamingo 3 (AF3)
it flips 62.5 % 62.5\% of true positives vs. 41.5 % 41.5\% for random, and a
synthetic oracle control disentangles model dependence from CLAP
localization error. At decoding time, a language-prior contrast lifts
Qwen2-Audio’s accuracy from 57.1 % 57.1\% to 68.2 % 68.2\% , beating AAD, and to 71.9 % 71.9\% (cross-validated) once combined and gated. A unified causal
profile does not transfer between models; Qwen2.5-Omni-7B
replicates Qwen2-Audio’s pattern, not AF3’s. Code: github.com/khalooei/causa .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large audio-language models (LALMs) such as Qwen2-Audio [ 5 ] and SALMONN [ 18 ] answer free-form questions about audio content but frequently exhibit object hallucination : confidently claiming a sound event is present when it is not [ 11 , 12 ] . The current inference-time mitigation, Audio-Aware Decoding (AAD) [ 10 ] , contrasts the model’s logits with real audio against logits from an all-zero “blank” waveform, almost certainly out-of-distribution for the audio encoder: the contrast conflates “evidence absent” with “input malformed.” We address this limitation with a more surgical intervention: localize the spectro-temporal region a claim’s evidence would occupy with sliding-window CLAP (Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining) similarity, then physically remove only that region via spectral gating, leaving the rest of the real, in-distribution recording untouched. This is a necessity test in the sense of Pearl’s Probability of Necessity [ 16 , 19 ] : if a claim survives removal of its own best-matching evidence, it was not grounded in that evidence. We complement it with a sufficiency test (inserting a real exemplar into a genuine negative-control clip) that validates the pipeline’s sensitivity. Unlike concurrent causal work that needs gradient or internal-activation access [ 9 , 3 , 4 , 1 ] , our test is fully black-box and training-free. On Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct, localized ablation’s raw AUROC trails blank’s; we show this is a duration confound that reverses once duration is held fixed (Section 5.1 ). On NVIDIA Audio Flamingo 3 [ 8 ] and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B [ 23 ] , raw detection value remains model-dependent.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Object hallucination in LALMs. Kuan et al. [ 11 ] introduce the object-existence discriminative-QA benchmark used here; a follow-up [ 12 ] broadens this to temporal-order/attribute hallucinations. AAD [ 10 ] is the closest prior mitigation, our baseline. Causal sufficiency/necessity, and white-box audio grounding. COPO [ 9 ] trains a causal-completeness reward via RL on image patches, needing training access; concurrent audio work traces causal effects layer-by-layer [ 3 ] , reads activations under silence/unrelated-audio substitution [ 4 ] , or trains a frame-level head [ 1 ] . Our tests need no training and intervene on raw audio only. Content-free calibration and adaptive contrastive decoding. Zhao et al. [ 25 ] calibrate against a content-free input; M3ID [ 6 ] contrasts an image-absent baseline, structurally identical to our Section 3.2 analysis (adapted to audio, not novel). VCD [ 13 ] /ICD [ 20 ] contrast a distorted input, closer to our localized/random ablation. Concurrently, TCD [ 15 ] gates a temporally-blurred contrast by uncertainty/audio-reliance and TAD [ 2 ] gates a silence contrast by token-level confidence; both gate when to apply one fixed contrast, where Section 5.5 instead scales how much of a language-prior contrast to apply.

sections.heading: 3.1 Necessity: localized spectral-gate ablation
sections.text: For a claim “yes” to “is there a sound of o o in the audio?”, we slide a window (2 s or 4 s, 0.5 s hop) over the clip and score each against “a sound of o o ” using LAION-CLAP [ 21 ] , taking the highest-similarity window as R ⁡ ( o ) R(o) . We attenuate energy within R ⁡ ( o ) R(o) by − 40 -40 or − 100 -100 dB via Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) masking with a 50 ms raised-cosine edge fade, leaving the rest of the waveform untouched, and re-query the model (e.g. a true-positive “laughter” claim: gating the CLAP-localized region flips it, P ⁡ ( yes ) P(\text{yes}) : 0.905 → 0.133 0.905\to 0.133 , while an equal-size random window does not).

sections.heading: 3.2 Controls
sections.text: Random-window. Same ablation, same size/depth, on a uniformly random window instead of CLAP’s choice. Blank-audio (AAD’s baseline [ 10 ] ). An all-zero waveform, scored identically. Language-only. No audio content block at all (not silence), giving the object-conditioned “yes” prior independent of any clip. Real-unrelated-audio substitution. Following [ 4 ] , the clip is replaced entirely with a different real, verified-negative recording, reproduced here fully black-box. Sufficiency. For “no” claims on a negative-control clip, we mix a real exemplar of the target class (CLAP-localized from a separate positive clip) in at matched loudness and re-query, checking whether the claim flips. Scoring. Every condition is scored identically: a single forward pass yields next-token log-probabilities for “yes”/“no”, renormalized over the forced choice to give P ⁡ ( yes ) P(\text{yes}) , deterministic, with no sampling.

sections.heading: 3.3 Oracle-localization control
sections.text: The grid above ablates only CLAP’s guess at the evidence location, so a null result is consistent with two mechanisms: the claim does not depend on any specific region, or CLAP’s guess is wrong enough that ablating it resembles ablating random. We disentangle these by inserting a real exemplar into a negative-control clip at a random but recorded offset, keeping only mixtures the model affirms, and ablating three same-size windows on the same mixture: the true insertion window ( oracle ), CLAP’s own top pick ( clap ), and a uniform random window ( random ), all at − 100 -100 dB, also reporting the temporal Intersection-over-Union (IoU) between CLAP’s window and the true one: a pure localization-accuracy number real clips cannot provide.

sections.heading: 3.4 From detection to mitigation: contrastive decoding
sections.text: Contrastive decoding [ 14 ] (and its instantiations AAD [ 10 ] and VCD/ICD/M3ID [ 13 , 20 , 6 ] ) uses a contrast to correct the answer at decoding time: d adj = ( 1 + α ) ​ logit ​ ( p yes real ) − α ​ logit ​ ( p yes contrast ) d_{\text{adj}}=(1+\alpha)\,\mathrm{logit}(p_{\text{yes}}^{\text{real}})-\alpha\,\mathrm{logit}(p_{\text{yes}}^{\text{contrast}}) (1) with logit ⁡ ( p ) = log ⁡ p 1 − p \mathrm{logit}(p)=\log\frac{p}{1-p} , answer “yes” iff d adj > 0 d_{\text{adj}}>0 . Reusing already-computed logits, we evaluate three contrasts: AAD-CD (blank audio), LangPrior-CD (Section 3.2 , M3ID-style), CAUSA-CD (the grid’s strongest localized cell), sweeping α ∈ [ 0 , 3 ] \alpha\in[0,3] and reporting the literature-standard α = 1 \alpha{=}1 to avoid cherry-picking. Our best rule (Section 5.5 ) needs two forward passes per query (real, blank); the language prior is a precomputed per- class constant.

sections.heading: 3.6 A causal grounding profile, and its identifiability
sections.text: Every quantity above answers a different question about the same claim: blank ​ - ​ drop \mathrm{blank\text{-}drop} asks whether any audio matters; Δ \Delta (Section 3.2 ) asks whether audio matters beyond the language prior ; the matched-control contrast asks whether the located region matters more than an equally-sized arbitrary one. We define the last as a specificity statistic, CS i = logit ⁡ ( p i rand ) − logit ⁡ ( p i loc ) \mathrm{CS}_{i}=\mathrm{logit}(p^{\text{rand}}_{i})-\mathrm{logit}(p^{\text{loc}}_{i}) , averaged over the four grid cells, and its graded analogue Δ loc \Delta_{\text{loc}} (Section 3.5 ), and collect all five signals into a per-claim profile z i = [ blank ​ - ​ drop i , clap ​ - ​ sim i , Δ i , CS i , Δ loc , i ] z_{i}=[\mathrm{blank\text{-}drop}_{i},\,\mathrm{clap\text{-}sim}_{i},\,\Delta_{i},\,\mathrm{CS}_{i},\,\Delta_{\text{loc},i}] . What this can and cannot identify. Waveform deletion implements do ⁡ ( E o := 0 ) \mathrm{do}(E_{o}{:=}0) only if the removed span is the only causal channel disturbed. Under a window-exchangeability null (the CLAP span carries no more claim-relevant information than a size-matched random span), 𝔼 ⁡ [ CS i ] = 0 \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{CS}_{i}]=0 ; a nonzero CS ^ \hat{\mathrm{CS}} rejects it but does not prove identification (CLAP bias toward salient spans would also give CS > 0 \mathrm{CS}>0 ), hence Section 5.3 ’s synthetic control with known true location.

sections.heading: 4 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Models. Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct [ 5 ] is the primary subject; NVIDIA Audio Flamingo 3 [ 8 ] (Whisper-style encoder, Qwen2.5-7B decoder) and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B [ 23 ] (Qwen2-Audio’s lineage, newer/larger) are cross-model checks. All three queried identically black-box. Data. The object-existence split of [ 12 ] 1 1 1 HF: kuanhuggingface/Audio-Hallucination_Object-Existence_AudioCaps-ESC50-VocalSound. , 10,800 rows, 53 classes from AudioCaps/ESC-50/VocalSound. Qwen2-Audio ( n = 5000 n{=}5000 , seed 42) yields 4355 affirmative claims (2488 correct, 1867 hallucinated, 43 % 43\% overclaim rate). AF3 affirms far less (needed an explicit “answer only Yes or No” suffix; even so 11.0 % 11.0\% vs. Qwen2-Audio’s 87.1 % 87.1\% ), so we draw the full n = 10,800 n{=}10{,}800 , yielding 1192 affirmative claims (1109 correct, 83 hallucinated, 93.0 % 93.0\% precision). Qwen2.5-Omni ( n = 2000 n{=}2000 ) yields 1774 affirmative claims (1022 correct, 752 hallucinated). The oracle control (§ 3.3 ) reuses the same benchmark’s negative-control rows and exemplar bank; no new data source. Metrics. AUROC/AUPRC for hallucinated-vs-correct separation; empirical P ​ N ^ \hat{PN} / P ​ S ^ \hat{PS} ; 2000-resample bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs). AF3’s small hallucinated count is well-powered at full-benchmark scale ( n = 83 n{=}83 hallucinated, 1109 1109 true positives) but its per-cell AUROC ranges widely ( 0.37 0.37 – 0.58 0.58 ); flip-rate is the reliable metric for this model.

sections.heading: 5.2 Graded necessity: thresholding costs the detector
sections.text: The adaptive search (§ 3.5 ) on all 4355 Qwen2-Audio examples confirms the localization theory: paired localization efficiency is real, Δ ^ loc = 0.028 \widehat{\Delta}_{\text{loc}}=0.028 (Wilcoxon p = 4.1 × 10 − 27 p{=}4.1\times 10^{-27} ; CI [ 0.023 , 0.033 ] [0.023,0.033] ): CLAP’s ranking reliably finds sufficient evidence with less removal than a blind search. This hides heterogeneity: splitting classes into acoustically transient vs. continuous/ambient , Δ loc \Delta_{\text{loc}} is several times larger for transient ( 0.116 0.116 vs. 0.017 0.017 , Mann–Whitney p = 3.1 × 10 − 15 p{=}3.1\times 10^{-15} ), independently reproduced in the oracle control below, and Table 1 ’s headline gap splits the same way, narrower on transient classes ( + 8.1 +8.1 AUROC points) than continuous ( + 16.8 +16.8 ): a real, substantial, but partial closing of the gap. R ^ ∗ \hat{R}^{\ast} itself is, surprisingly, a chance-level detector (AUROC = 0.491 =0.491 ): 89 % 89\% of true positives/hallucinations never flip even after near-total coverage, so the binary statistic discards the graded confidence change along the way. The continuous P ⁡ ( yes ) P(\text{yes}) drop at the final checkpoint recovers it (AUROC = 0.651 =0.651 ): a clean causal quantity and a good detector are not automatically the same once censored. On AF3, efficiency is an order of magnitude larger ( Δ ^ loc = 0.195 \widehat{\Delta}_{\text{loc}}{=}0.195 ), censoring nearly eliminated, yet R ^ ∗ \hat{R}^{\ast} stays chance-level (AUROC = 0.52 =0.52 ): removal amount needed and early resistance to removal are related but distinct signals, unreliable for AF3 at any scale.

sections.heading: 5.3 Oracle-localization control: is the null a localizer artifact?
sections.text: Table 2: Oracle control, synthetic Qwen2-Audio positives with known evidence location ( n = 608 n{=}608 , − 100 -100 dB, matched size). Oracle CLAP Random Flip rate 16.8% 10.5% 3.1% Mean P ⁡ ( yes ) P(\text{yes}) drop 0.126 0.079 0.016 Mean CLAP–true-location IoU: 0.45 (25% zero-overlap). Table 2 answers the question Section 5.1 leaves open: is Qwen2-Audio’s near-flat gap because CLAP finds the wrong region, or because the model does not depend on any specific region even when known exactly? Both. CLAP’s guess only moderately overlaps the true region (mean IoU 0.45; 25% zero overlap), and ablating the true location beats ablating CLAP’s guess by a wide, significant margin (16.8% vs. 10.5%, CI [ 4.1 , 8.4 ] [4.1,8.4] ), which beats random (10.5% vs. 3.1%, CI [ 4.9 , 9.9 ] [4.9,9.9] ): a real share of the near-null result is a localizer-accuracy artifact. But even the true location flips only 16.8% of these claims, far below blank’s near-total effect: genuine, partial location-insensitivity survives this control too.

sections.heading: 5.4 Language-prior correction: ensemble significant, alone it isn’t
sections.text: Querying each class with no audio block gives mean language-only P ⁡ ( yes ) = 0.935 P(\text{yes})=0.935 for true positives, 0.928 0.928 for hallucinations, nearly identical (AUROC = 0.490 =0.490 , chance): the model leans “yes” ≈ 93 % \approx\!93\% of the time regardless of object. Correcting for this, Δ = P ( yes ∣ real ) − P ( yes ∣ no audio ) \Delta=P(\text{yes}\mid\text{real})-P(\text{yes}\mid\text{no audio}) gives AUROC = 0.727 =0.727 ; a 3-feature ensemble (blank-drop, CLAP, Δ \Delta ; 5-fold cross-validation (CV)) reaches 0.743 0.743 . Δ \Delta alone doesn’t beat blank-audio (CI [ − 0.009 , 0.020 ] [-0.009,0.020] ); the ensemble does per-example ( + 0.022 +0.022 , CI [ 0.011 , 0.033 ] [0.011,0.033] ) but not per-class (CI [ − 0.043 , 0.046 ] [-0.043,0.046] ). Adding substitution [ 4 ] as a fourth feature does not help (AUROC = 0.646 =0.646 alone; 4-feature ensemble statistically flat at 0.743 0.743 ), redundant rather than complementary; the full 5-feature profile (Table 1 ) plateaus at the same 0.743 0.743 .

Decoding-side, its overclaiming is far less language-prior-driven (AAD-CD/LangPrior-CD move accuracy by only + 0.7 +0.7 / + 0.3 +0.3 pp), but CAUSA-CD, weakest for Qwen2-Audio, gives this model’s largest single-contrast gain ( + 1.6 +1.6 pp).

sections.heading: 5.7 Cross-model transfer of the causal grounding profile
sections.text: If grounding failure has a common causal structure, a detector trained on one model’s profile z z (§ 3.6 ) should transfer to another’s. In-distribution, a 5-fold CV ensemble over z z only modestly beats its best single signal on Qwen-Audio ( 0.743 0.743 vs. 0.727 0.727 , CI crosses zero by-class) and underperforms on AF3 ( − 9.9 -9.9 pp), with only 83 AF3 hallucinations, so it overfits noise. The sharper test: standardize z z within each model, fit the logistic router on one, score the other without retraining . Both directions lose to the target’s own best fixed contrast (Qwen → \to AF3: − 1.4 -1.4 pp; AF3 → \to Qwen: − 13.1 -13.1 pp), a genuine negative result: the two failure modes differ qualitatively (language-prior override vs. coarse localization sensitivity).

sections.heading: 6 Discussion, Limitations, and Conclusion
sections.text: Limitations. Qwen2-Audio’s weak localized-vs-random gap (§ 5.3 ) is only partly a CLAP-accuracy artifact; the language-prior ensemble’s significance holds per-example, not per-class; we do not correct for multiple comparisons. Qwen2.5-Omni has only headline numbers; Phi-4-multimodal and FLAM [ 22 ] remain non-functional (dependency incompatibilities). On the shorter HalluAudio benchmark [ 24 ] ( 3.8 3.8 s vs. 10.0 10.0 s median), § 5.1 ’s matched-duration effect attenuates sharply, though a small residual survives on Qwen2-Audio ( p = 8.9 × 10 − 5 p{=}8.9\times 10^{-5} ). Combined-decoding (§ 5.5 ) replicates cleanly regardless ( 81.2 % ± 2.4 81.2\%\pm 2.4 vs. 80.1 % ± 2.1 80.1\%\pm 2.1 ). Conclusion. Localization’s raw detection value is model- and class-dependent, but its weakness on Qwen2-Audio is a duration confound: holding duration fixed, localized removal decisively beats a matched random window on both models (§ 5.1 ). A single causal grounding profile does not transfer across models (§ 5.7 ). Together with a validated decoding-time correction, this is our contribution.

sections.heading: Compliance with Ethical Standards
sections.text: This study uses only publicly released benchmark audio (AudioCaps, ESC-50, VocalSound, via [ 12 ] ) and openly released pretrained models; it involves no new data collection from human or animal subjects and required no institutional ethical review.

A Black-Box Causal Audit Reveals Model-Dependent Audio Grounding in LALM Hallucination Mohammad Khalooei 1,2 Mohammad Sabokrou 3,4 Abstract Large audio-language models (LALMs) frequently hallucinate sounds that are not present. Audio-Aware Decoding (AAD) [ 10 ] contrasts logits under the real recording against an all-zero “blank” waveform, which is out-of-distribution and conflates “evidence absent” with “input malformed.” We introduce a black-box causal test: localize the region a claim would rely on with CLAP, remove only that region via spectral gating, and compare against an equally-sized random window, on three LALMs. On Qwen2-Audio-7B ( n = 4355 n{=}4355 ), localized ablation’s raw AUROC trails blank’s (0.613 vs. 0.721); we show this is a duration confound: a duration-only regression predicts blank’s mean effect almost exactly ( 0.067 0.067 vs. 0.071 0.071 ), and holding duration fixed, localized ablation beats random removal at every grid cell, on both models. On Audio Flamingo 3 (AF3) it flips 62.5 % 62.5\% of true positives vs. 41.5 % 41.5\% for random, and a synthetic oracle control disentangles model dependence from CLAP localization error. At decoding time, a language-prior contrast lifts Qwen2-Audio’s accuracy from 57.1 % 57.1\% to 68.2 % 68.2\% , beating AAD, and to 71.9 % 71.9\% (cross-validated) once combined and gated. A unified causal profile does not transfer between models; Qwen2.5-Omni-7B replicates Qwen2-Audio’s pattern, not AF3’s. Code: github.com/khalooei/causa . Index Terms: audio-language models, hallucination detection, causal ablation, black-box interpretability, model comparison † † address: 1 Sharif University of Technology, Iran 2 Amirkabir University of Technology, Iran 3 New Uzbekistan University, Uzbekistan 4 Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology, Japan 1 Introduction Large audio-language models (LALMs) such as Qwen2-Audio [ 5 ] and SALMONN [ 18 ] answer free-form questions about audio content but frequently exhibit object hallucination : confidently claiming a sound event is present when it is not [ 11 , 12 ] . The current inference-time mitigation, Audio-Aware Decoding (AAD) [ 10 ] , contrasts the model’s logits with real audio against logits from an all-zero “blank” waveform, almost certainly out-of-distribution for the audio encoder: the contrast conflates “evidence absent” with “input malformed.” We address this limitation with a more surgical intervention: localize the spectro-temporal region a claim’s evidence would occupy with sliding-window CLAP (Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining) similarity, then physically remove only that region via spectral gating, leaving the rest of the real, in-distribution recording untouched. This is a necessity test in the sense of Pearl’s Probability of Necessity [ 16 , 19 ] : if a claim survives removal of its own best-matching evidence, it was not grounded in that evidence. We complement it with a sufficiency test (inserting a real exemplar into a genuine negative-control clip) that validates the pipeline’s sensitivity. Unlike concurrent causal work that needs gradient or internal-activation access [ 9 , 3 , 4 , 1 ] , our test is fully black-box and training-free. On Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct, localized ablation’s raw AUROC trails blank’s; we show this is a duration confound that reverses once duration is held fixed (Section 5.1 ). On NVIDIA Audio Flamingo 3 [ 8 ] and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B [ 23 ] , raw detection value remains model-dependent. 2 Related Work Object hallucination in LALMs. Kuan et al. [ 11 ] introduce the object-existence discriminative-QA benchmark used here; a follow-up [ 12 ] broadens this to temporal-order/attribute hallucinations. AAD [ 10 ] is the closest prior mitigation, our baseline. Causal sufficiency/necessity, and white-box audio grounding. COPO [ 9 ] trains a causal-completeness reward via RL on image patches, needing training access; concurrent audio work traces causal effects layer-by-layer [ 3 ] , reads activations under silence/unrelated-audio substitution [ 4 ] , or trains a frame-level head [ 1 ] . Our tests need no training and intervene on raw audio only. Content-free calibration and adaptive contrastive decoding. Zhao et al. [ 25 ] calibrate against a content-free input; M3ID [ 6 ] contrasts an image-absent baseline, structurally identical to our Section 3.2 analysis (adapted to audio, not novel). VCD [ 13 ] /ICD [ 20 ] contrast a distorted input, closer to our localized/random ablation. Concurrently, TCD [ 15 ] gates a temporally-blurred contrast by uncertainty/audio-reliance and TAD [ 2 ] gates a silence contrast by token-level confidence; both gate when to apply one fixed contrast, where Section 5.5 instead scales how much of a language-prior contrast to apply. 3 Method 3.1 Necessity: localized spectral-gate ablation For a claim “yes” to “is there a sound of o o in the audio?”, we slide a window (2 s or 4 s, 0.5 s hop) over the clip and score each against “a sound of o o ” using LAION-CLAP [ 21 ] , taking the highest-similarity window as R ⁡ ( o ) R(o) . We attenuate energy within R ⁡ ( o ) R(o) by − 40 -40 or − 100 -100 dB via Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) masking with a 50 ms raised-cosine edge fade, leaving the rest of the waveform untouched, and re-query the model (e.g. a true-positive “laughter” claim: gating the CLAP-localized region flips it, P ⁡ ( yes ) P(\text{yes}) : 0.905 → 0.133 0.905\to 0.133 , while an equal-size random window does not). 3.2 Controls Random-window. Same ablation, same size/depth, on a uniformly random window instead of CLAP’s choice. Blank-audio (AAD’s baseline [ 10 ] ). An all-zero waveform, scored identically. Language-only. No audio content block at all (not silence), giving the object-conditioned “yes” prior independent of any clip. Real-unrelated-audio substitution. Following [ 4 ] , the clip is replaced entirely with a different real, verified-negative recording, reproduced here fully black-box. Sufficiency. For “no” claims on a negative-control clip, we mix a real exemplar of the target class (CLAP-localized from a separate positive clip) in at matched loudness and re-query, checking whether the claim flips. Scoring. Every condition is scored identically: a single forward pass yields next-token log-probabilities for “yes”/“no”, renormalized over the forced choice to give P ⁡ ( yes ) P(\text{yes}) , deterministic, with no sampling. 3.3 Oracle-localization control The grid above ablates only CLAP’s guess at the evidence location, so a null result is consistent with two mechanisms: the claim does not depend on any specific region, or CLAP’s guess is wrong enough that ablating it resembles ablating random. Qwen2-Audio’s weak localized-vs-random gap (§ 5.3 ) is only partly a CLAP-accuracy artifact; the language-prior ensemble’s significance holds per-example, not per-class; we do not correct for multiple comparisons. Qwen2.5-Omni has only headline numbers; Phi-4-multimodal and FLAM [ 22 ] remain non-functional (dependency incompatibilities). On the shorter HalluAudio benchmark [ 24 ] ( 3.8 3.8 s vs. 10.0 10.0 s median), § 5.1 ’s matched-duration effect attenuates sharply, though a small residual survives on Qwen2-Audio ( p = 8.9 × 10 − 5 p{=}8.9\times 10^{-5} ). Combined-decoding (§ 5.5 ) replicates cleanly regardless ( 81.2 % ± 2.4 81.2\%\pm 2.4 vs. 80.1 % ± 2.1 80.1\%\pm 2.1 ). Conclusion. Localization’s raw detection value is model- and class-dependent, but its weakness on Qwen2-Audio is a duration confound: holding duration fixed, localized removal decisively beats a matched random window on both models (§ 5.1 ). A single causal grounding profile does not transfer across models (§ 5.7 ). Together with a validated decoding-time correction, this is our contribution.
